parity_risks.note: The deferred balance carries from one row to the next inside a customer, so RECOGNIZED and DEFERRED depend on the order the rows are processed in. The script fixes that order itself with `sort_values(["CUSTOMER", "PERIOD"])`, and (CUSTOMER, PERIOD) is unique on the incoming stream in every golden set, so the sort is total and the result is reproducible.

A cancelled period resets the carried balance to zero BEFORE that period's own cap is applied, so a cancellation is visible in RECOGNIZED as well as in DEFERRED. broken_sql/seg_02/01_cancellation_reset_ignored.py is that rule removed.

pandas `groupby` drops rows whose key is NULL, so a NULL CUSTOMER would silently vanish rather than form its own schedule -- which is why CUSTOMER is declared NOT NULL on this stream. Nothing upstream guarantees a non-NULL CUSTOMER; the Filter only guarantees BILLED.

A NULL CAP is silently NOT a cap: `float(NULL)` is `nan` on both engines and `min(x, nan)` returns `x`, so the row recognizes everything billed and carries nothing forward. Both sides do the identical thing, so parity holds and no diff would ever surface it -- it is a data-quality risk in the source, recorded here rather than guarded against.

A NULL CANCELLED is where the two engines disagree by default: the simulator types the column as pandas `boolean`, where `bool(pd.NA)` raises, while the Local Testing Framework's `to_pandas()` yields `None`, where `bool(None)` is quietly `False`. A migration must not turn a loud failure into silent output, so `proc.py` tests `pd.isna(row["CANCELLED"])` and raises -- the procedure fails on exactly the row the Alteryx script fails on, and `validate_snowpark.py` would report it as a FAIL. No golden set carries such a row: the simulator cannot build one, because the Python tool raises before it can be written. How REAL Alteryx types a NULL Bool field inside the Python tool is UNVERIFIED -- the simulator's nullable dtype is this project's assumption, not an observation.

Both sides compute in IEEE doubles and round to 2 decimals with Python's own `round`, which is round-half-to-even on the binary value -- not the half-away-from-zero Alteryx uses in its formula engine. That agreement is only guaranteed because the same Python expression runs on both sides; a SQL rewrite of this tool would not round the same way.
